o: Report users having at least one 'Refinance' loan AND at least one 'Mortgage' loan. Only user 102 qualifies in the example. Two natural formulations: intersect two IN-subqueries, or GROUP BY user with HAVING over conditional counts.
k: Both conditions are existence checks per user.
COUNT(DISTINCT loan_type) guards against duplicated rows.
IN-subquery intersection mirrors the logical AND directly.

a.i: Select distinct users appearing in the Refinance subset and in the Mortgage subset.
s: Filter Loans for loan_type = 'Refinance' and collect user_ids.

c.python:
-- MySQL
SELECT DISTINCT user_id
FROM Loans
WHERE user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM Loans WHERE loan_type = 'Refinance')
  AND user_id IN (SELECT user_id FROM Loans WHERE loan_type = 'Mortgage')
ORDER BY user_id;

a.t: O(L log L) — two filtered scans plus a sort for DISTINCT/order.

a.n: GROUP BY with HAVING conditional counts
a.i: Group all loans by user and require SUM(loan_type='Refinance') > 0 and SUM(loan_type='Mortgage') > 0 in HAVING.

c.python:
-- MySQL
SELECT user_id
FROM Loans
GROUP BY user_id
HAVING SUM(loan_type = 'Refinance') > 0
   AND SUM(loan_type = 'Mortgage') > 0
ORDER BY user_id;

w: MySQL treats booleans as 0/1, enabling the SUM trick; in other dialects use COUNT(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 END). GROUP BY user_id alone suffices since grouping implies distinctness — no outer DISTINCT needed. Follow-up: users with exactly these two types and no others, or per-type counts.
